newsitem.title: UK: CBI shows feel-good factor on the horizon - analysts.
newsitem.headline: CBI shows feel-good factor on the horizon - analysts.

text.p: A surge in British retail activity in August reported by the Confederation of British Industry on Thursday is further evidence the feel-good factor is on its way back, analysts said.
"These are very high numbers and proof people are very eager to spend their cash," said Michael Dicks, UK economist at Lehman Brothers.
"Sales are up across the board, stocks are tumbling and, looking ahead, retailers expect activity to move up another gear, so this is not temporary thing."
The CBI said retail sales volume rose again in August and the balance of firms reporting an increase in business was the largest since November 1988.
Dicks said the ongoing consumer spending spree was not just good news for retailers. "Orders to factories are up which will help the manufacturing sector."
Orders placed with suppliers rose markedly for the second month in a row following a run down in stocks which are now at their lowest level since January 1992, the CBI said.

Philip Shaw, group economist at Union Plc, agreed the whole economy stands to benefit from the high street boom. "The survey suggests the economy shoudd enjoy a consumer driven bounce back this year."

He said higher incomes are behind the spurt in consumer activity and, since tax rises came to an end last year and income tax was cut in the budget, households are holding on to all of their pay rises.
Hopes of more tax cuts to come this year and the ongoing windfall payments from building society mergers and floatations look set to keep consumer confidence running high.
But the price rises reported in the CBI survey gives some analysts cause for concern.
"With very strong demand and stocks dropping, those shops which have not already put up prices will do so pretty quickly," said Dicks.
"In that case, the floor for RPI is not that far away. We should get good figures for August and maybe September, but then it could turn."
Shaw said falling cost pressures would, to an extent, limit retail price increases.
"Prices in the survey were certainly a bit stronger than expected, but the superb drop in producer prices is still to feed through and that should keep a lid on retail prices for a while," he said.
The CBI said the reported pick-up in selling prices was from a low base. The rises reflected cost increases going back several months.
"Retailers have held off as long as they can," said Alastair Eperon, head of the CBI's distributive traders panel. "Price competition conintues to be very strong indeed on the high street."
Nevertheless, on Thursday, electrical goods retailer Dixons also reported sales dramatically up this year. Like-for-like sales were up 11 percent in the first 18 weeks of its current financial year.
But car sales rose by just 2.2 percent year-on-year in what is normally the peak sales month of August according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders.
"There's no need to fear an increase in inflation yet," Eperon at the CBI said. We're certainly not seeing 1980s-style boom conditions."
